name: ifb_context_cache
description: Context-cache IFB trace. c0..c2 share one system prompt through the chat template: c1 arrives while c0 decodes (partial hit on the system pages), c2 repeats c0 after it finishes (hit on every full page of c0's prompt). m1/m2 are a chat-template conversation whose second turn reuses the first turn's pages. h0..h2 are one conversation written as raw ChatML so that each turn extends the previous turn's prompt exactly; earlier answers are fixed text so every turn's prompt is the same in the run and the reference (the hybrid cache matches exact prompt-end snapshots, and the Qwen3.5 template re-renders earlier assistant turns without their think block); its history passes max_input_len = 1024 from the second turn on, so only the uncached tail runs, chunked under mixed. x0 is a 717-token prompt that arrives while h1 decodes and is cancelled one h1 token later (under mixed, best effort between its 512-token chunk and its final chunk); x1 repeats it afterwards and must compute it in full and match the reference: when x0's prompt did not complete, x1 must reuse nothing (a cancelled prompt publishes nothing). Full-attention hits are page-granular (the min bounds are the full pages shared with the earlier requests); hybrid hits only at published snapshot lengths, so the shared-system-prompt hits carry no hybrid lower bound and only the h turns, which extend the previous turn's prompt exactly, keep theirs.

snippets.bees: A honeybee colony behaves almost like a single organism. The queen lays eggs, sometimes more than a thousand in a day, while thousands of workers divide the remaining tasks according to their age. Young workers clean cells and feed larvae, middle-aged bees build wax comb and guard the entrance, and the oldest bees fly out to collect nectar and pollen. A forager that finds a rich patch of flowers returns to the hive and performs a waggle dance whose angle and duration tell her sisters the direction and distance of the food. In winter the colony forms a tight cluster and the bees shiver their flight muscles to keep the center warm, slowly eating the honey they stored during summer.
snippets.bread: Baking bread is a lesson in patience and chemistry. Flour, water, salt, and yeast are mixed into a dough, and kneading stretches the gluten proteins into a network that can hold gas. As the yeast feeds on sugars it releases carbon dioxide, and the dough slowly rises. A long, cool fermentation develops more flavor than a quick, warm one, which is why many bakers prepare their dough the night before. In the oven the trapped gas expands, the starches set, and the surface browns as sugars and proteins react to form a crisp crust. Sourdough bakers replace commercial yeast with a living starter of wild yeast and bacteria, which gives the loaf its tangy taste and chewy texture.
snippets.currents: The oceans are never still. Winds push the surface water into great circular currents called gyres, and the rotation of the earth bends these flows to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern. Deep below the surface a slower circulation is driven by differences in temperature and salt. Near the poles, cold salty water sinks and spreads along the sea floor, while warmer water moves toward the poles to replace it. This global conveyor carries heat from the tropics to higher latitudes and helps keep some coastal regions much milder than their latitude would suggest. Changes in this circulation could alter rainfall, storm tracks, and sea level along many coasts.
snippets.libraries: Public libraries began as small collections shared by members who paid a subscription, but during the nineteenth century many cities opened libraries free to everyone. The idea was simple and radical: anyone, regardless of income, should be able to read, study, and learn. Librarians developed classification systems so that readers could find a book on any subject, and card catalogs filled long wooden cabinets. Today libraries lend not only books but also music, films, and digital resources, and they offer quiet places to work, internet access, and classes for children and adults. In many neighborhoods the library is one of the few indoor public spaces where people can stay as long as they like without buying anything.
snippets.lighthouses: Before satellites and radio, sailors relied on lighthouses to find their way along dangerous coasts. Early towers burned wood or coal in open fires, which gave a weak and smoky light. Later builders used oil lamps with polished reflectors, and in the nineteenth century the Fresnel lens changed everything: rings of glass prisms bent the light into a narrow beam that could be seen more than twenty miles away. Each lighthouse was given its own pattern of flashes so that a navigator could identify it at night. Keepers lived at the stations with their families, trimming wicks, winding clockwork, and recording the weather. Most lights are automated today, but many towers still stand as landmarks and museums.
snippets.railways: The first public railways appeared in the early nineteenth century, and within a few decades they had changed how people thought about distance and time. Goods that once took weeks to move by canal or road could cross a country in a day. Towns along the new lines grew quickly, while places the tracks avoided often declined. Railways also forced countries to adopt standard time, because every town keeping its own local noon made timetables impossible to read. Building the lines required enormous effort: workers dug cuttings and tunnels by hand, raised embankments across marshes, and threw iron bridges over rivers. Many of those routes are still in use, now carrying electric trains at speeds the early engineers could hardly imagine.
snippets.rivers: Rivers shape the land they cross. Over thousands of years a river carves its valley, carries sand and silt downstream, and builds wide plains where it slows down near the sea. When the current loses speed at the mouth, the sediment settles and forms a delta, a fan of channels and islands that shifts with every flood. Farmers have settled on these plains since the earliest villages because the soil is fertile and water is close, but the same floods that bring new soil can also destroy homes and fields. Engineers now build levees, reservoirs, and spillways to control the water, yet each change upstream alters how the river moves sediment, and the delta downstream slowly responds to those changes.
snippets.volcanoes: A volcano forms where molten rock from deep inside the earth finds a path to the surface. Some volcanoes erupt gently, with rivers of runny lava that flow for miles and slowly build broad shield-shaped mountains. Others explode violently because their thick magma traps gas until the pressure becomes too great, throwing ash high into the atmosphere. Large eruptions can cool the climate for a year or more, as fine particles in the upper air reflect sunlight back into space. Scientists watch active volcanoes with seismometers, gas sensors, and satellite measurements of the ground surface, looking for the small swelling and earthquakes that often come before an eruption. Even so, predicting the exact timing remains difficult.
snippets.answer_m1: Rivers shape valleys and carry sediment to the sea. Lighthouses evolved from wood fires to automated lamps that still guide ships. Bees organize their hives around a queen and pollinate many crops.
snippets.answer_h0: Rivers carve their valleys and move sediment downstream. Lighthouses grew from open fires into automated beacons. Bees and railways both show how carefully organized networks move what a community needs.
snippets.answer_h1: Volcanoes, libraries and ocean currents all move or preserve something over long spans of time, much like the rivers, lighthouses, bees and railways from the first message.
